=Knuth Volume 1: Fundamental Algorithms=

==Chapter 1: Basic Concepts: Binomial Coefficients==

===Definitions===

The combinations of n objects taken k at a time are the possible choices of k different elements from a collection of n items. The number is the binomial coefficient C(n,k) = n!/(k!(n-k)!). Computing these in a table gives Pascal's Triangle.

For non-integer n, define (AOCP V1 1.2.6 eq (3)):

C(r,k) = r(r-1)...(r-k+1) / (k(k-1)...1) = prod_{1<=j<=k} (r+1-j)/j,  k in Z, k>=0
C(r,k) = 0  for k < 0

Identities classify as: representation by factorials, symmetry, moving in/out of brackets, addition, summation, binomial theorem, negating upper index, sums of products.

===Representation by Factorials===

C(n,k) = n!/(k!(n-k)!)  for integers n, k>=0. (eq (5))

===Symmetry Condition===

C(n,k) = C(n,n-k)  for all integers k. (eq (6))

===Moving In and Out of Brackets===

C(r,k) = (r/k) C(r-1,k-1),  k != 0. (eq (7))
k C(r,k) = r C(r-1,k-1)   (all integers k)
C(r,k) = (r/(r-k)) C(r-1,k)   for k != r.

===Addition formulas===

C(r,k) = C(r-1,k) + C(r-1,k-1)  for integer k (eq (9)) -- sum of the two Pascal entries above-left and above-right.

===Summation formulas===

Summation identity 1 (repeated addition; "hockey stick") (eq (10)):
sum_{0<=k<=n} C(r+k,k) = C(r,0)+C(r+1,1)+...+C(r+n,n) = C(r+n+1,n),  n>=0

Summation identity 2 (eq (11)):
sum_{0<=k<=n} C(k,m) = C(0,m)+C(1,m)+...+C(n,m) = C(n+1,m+1),  integer m,n >= 0

===Deriving summation identities===

To compute 1^2 + 2^2 + ... + n^2, recognize k^2 = 2 C(k,2) + C(k,1), so
sum_{0<=k<=n} k^2 = 2 C(n+1,3) + C(n+1,2) = (1/3) n (n + 1/2)(n+1).
Any polynomial a_0 + a_1 k + ... + a_m k^m can be expressed as b_0 C(k,0) + ... + b_m C(k,m).

===Binomial Theorem===

(x+y)^r = sum_{0<=k<=r} C(r,k) x^k y^{r-k}  for integer r>=0 (eq (13)).
y=1 case: sum_k C(r,k) x^k = (1+x)^r  for integer r>=0 or |x|<1.
Newton discovered the binomial theorem in 1676; Euler attempted a proof in 1774; Gauss gave the first actual proof in 1812.
Abel's generalization (eq (16)): (x+y)^r = sum_k C(r,k) x(x-kz)^{k-1}(y+kz)^{r-k}, integer r>=0, x != 0.

===Negating Upper Index===

C(-r,k) = (-1)^k C(r+k-1,k),  k in Z. (eq (17))
Consequence: sum_{k<=n} C(r,k)(-1)^k = (-1)^n C(r-1,n)  for integer n>=0.
Proof: sum_{k<=n} C(r,k)(-1)^k = sum_{k<=n} C(-r+k-1,k) = C(-r+n,n) = (-1)^n C(r-1,n).
Also, for integer r: C(n,m) = (-1)^{n-m} C(-(m+1), n-m),  m,n in Z, n>=0.

===Simplifying Products===

C(r,m) C(m,k) = C(r,k) C(r-k,m-k),  integer m, k (eq (20)).

===Sums of Products===

Vandermonde's convolution (eq (21), published 1772) -- the most important, "should be memorized":

sum_k C(r,k) C(s,n-k) = C(r+s,n)

Interpret the RHS as choosing n people from r men and s women; each LHS term chooses k men and n-k women.

Further:
sum_k C(r,k) C(s,n+k) = C(r+s, r+n),  r,n in Z, r != 0
sum_k C(r,k) C(s+k,n) (-1)^k = (-1)^r C(s,n-r),  n,r in Z, r>=0

===Stirling Numbers===

Stirling numbers convert between powers and binomial coefficients (falling factorials). First kind [n m] (permutations of n letters with m cycles), second kind {n m} (partitions of n elements into m nonempty subsets). (Exercise 64)

First kind (falling factorial -> powers) (eq (40)): n! C(x,n) = x(x-1)...(x-n+1) = sum_k (-1)^{n-k} [n k] x^k
Second kind (powers -> binomials) (eq (41)): x^n = sum_k {n k} C(x,k) k!
Addition formulas (eq (42)): [n m] = (n-1)[n-1 m] + [n-1 m-1];  {n m} = m {n-1 m} + {n-1 m-1}, n>0.
Inversion formulas (eq (43)): sum_k [n k]{k m}(-1)^k = (-1)^n delta_{mn};  sum_k {n k}[k m](-1)^k = (-1)^n delta_{mn}.

=Example Problems=

==Knuth AOCP Section 1.2.6 Problem 36==

Sum of each row of Pascal's triangle: sum_k C(n,k) = 2^n.
Alternating signs: sum_k C(n,k)(-1)^k = (1-1)^n = 0^n = 0 for n>0, 1 for n=0.
Missing endpoints: sum_{k=1}^{n-1} C(n,k) = 2^n - 2 = 2(2^{n-1}-1).

==The Zeta Family==

Monogram (First Middle Last initials), no repeats, alphabetical order: choose 2 unique letters from 25 = C(25,2) = 300 = 24+23+...+1 = n(n-1)/2.

==Sum of Sequence==

For odd n>1, the sequence C(n,1),...,C(n,(n-1)/2) has an odd number of odd numbers.
By symmetry, sum_{k=1}^{(n-1)/2} C(n,k) = (1/2) sum_{k=1}^{n-1} C(n,k) = (1/2)(2^n - 2) = 2^{n-1} - 1, which is odd, proving the claim.
